Rajeev Singh
CEO, Al Maha Ceramics
Yeah. Hi. Good morning, everybody. I'm Rajeev Singh, CEO for Al Maha Ceramics, and along with my colleague, Mr. Vikas Shukla, who is my Finance Manager. I welcome all of you for saving your time and attending this meeting. Before we start, I will just show you one small presentation, though our figures are already public domain. I will take you through few of the slides so that it refreshes your memory on information on our company. After that, I think we'll take it up in terms of answering to your questions one by one. Over to Vikas. I think, Vikas, you can share your screens. Is it?
Vikas Shukla
Finance Manager, Al Maha Ceramics
Good morning, everyone.
Rajeev Singh
CEO, Al Maha Ceramics
Good morning.
Vikas Shukla
Finance Manager, Al Maha Ceramics
Hello. Good morning, everyone. This is our key highlights regarding the FY 2025, what is done as compared to the previous years. Company has done a tremendous performance and major turnaround in FY 2025 as compared to, if you see last two year, we are suffering with getting losses. That's the major turnaround. It reflects in our profitability as well as volume and everywhere. You see our revenue grew by 41%, and then profit grew by 120% in comparison to FY 2024. Recently we started our Al Hael, our sister company, its operation in November 2025. The highlights and quantitatives. This is sales revenue, means major key highlights. It's a comparison of FY 2024 versus FY 2025. Our key ratio analysis, similar FY 2024 versus 2025.
Rajeev Singh
CEO, Al Maha Ceramics
You can see that overall in all the parameters there has been an improvement, and that has resulted to the better results. Yes.
Vikas Shukla
Finance Manager, Al Maha Ceramics
These are income statement comparison FY 2024 versus 2025 in absolute value. This is sales and distribution overheads comparison, previous years versus current year in absolute value. Positions. Then admin overheads, element-wise. This is balance sheet comparison.
Rajeev Singh
CEO, Al Maha Ceramics
All of you guys are very much available, and yes, we are giving you a glimpse of that. Next. Cash flow.
Vikas Shukla
Finance Manager, Al Maha Ceramics
Cash flow comparison, previous years versus current.
Rajeev Singh
CEO, Al Maha Ceramics
I think, I'm sure there will be questions around this, what are the challenges? As you all are aware, we have just given the gist of our challenges, and we can discuss specifically on this, and then opportunities. Way forward, these are also something which you are aware of in terms of opportunities. Anti-dumping implementation by Oman government, but the effect will start visible now. Quality Mark implementation from 1 March. Of course there are new markets which are opening up like US, Jordan, Syria, and Iraq, a huge market. Due to the geopolitical situation, it gives you an opportunity to explore those markets. Internal factors where we are moving is like we are launching new value-added tiles in Al Maha. We have launched R12 Anti-Slip.
These are some of the products you will not find with the competition. These are very innovative and puts Al Maha on top of the chart in terms of the premium brand. Al Hael, we are planning to start Line 2 within next two to three months. Basically, we will be implementing those new innovative products which are fetching very high realization and very, very unique products which are not generally available with most of the competition. These are the way forward, and I'll open the floor for everybody. You can just raise your you know questions one by one. I will be trying to answer them. This is a small glimpse of presentation what we made though every figure is there in the public domain.
Just to refresh this, I thought. Yeah, you can go to the main screen. Abbas.
Abbas Al Lawati
SVP and Head of Project Management Office, Sohar International
Hi, Rajeev. Thank you for the call. Congratulations on a good year. Big turnaround from the year before that. I think, under your leadership, you guys managed to do quite well. Now, we have to move forward with the benefit of implementation of anti-dumping duty and also the quality standards. What kind of utilizations are you expecting in the ceramic plant? I'll come to Al Hael as a separate sort of question, but let's stick to the ceramic plant. What opportunities, what utilization are you looking at? You think Oman can absorb your capacity? Is there any disruptions to your export market? As part of that, the question comes on your raw material side, glazing material. Are you facing any challenges importing them into the country? Do you have enough inventory of them?
Do you expect any disruptions? Questions around your ceramic plant, naturally, that you expect from an analyst, and then I have some other specific questions that I'm gonna ask you as well. Thank you.
Rajeev Singh
CEO, Al Maha Ceramics
Thank you, Abbas. I'll go one by one. I think, anti-dumping was announced long back. As I was explaining to you during my one-to-one discussion with you, also that, unfortunately, we have given enough time to the local importers to bring in almost 5–6x more material than regular intake what Oman was taking, and that has resulted in further deterioration of the market. Even some of the stocks are still lying, but we are expecting that that should dissipate and it should start reflecting in our numbers for the domestic market. Now, anti-dumping is implemented on Chinese and Indian products because their volumes are high.
Nevertheless, we cannot overlook the very cheap imports coming from Saudi Arabia which has got a Chinese unit there, and they have gone for expansion and plus the prices are ridiculously low. This is disturbing the entire Middle East, not just Oman. Frankly speaking, as far as I am concerned, we have to live with the situation. Though it is a facilitating factor for a company, but in my experience of 30 years, these challenges are always there. Whether there is sometimes Chinese jumping in or maybe Indian. We have to really create a market for ourselves, and that way I will not say that I will be depending solely on these factors, external factors to drive my performance for the coming years.
As for the capacity utilization you asked, I think that we should reach 80%-84% this year. That's what we are planning. An improvement should be seen by the end of this quarter because I think Ramadan and everything has come and it is now getting over. Now we should start seeing the market opening up. Coming to the present, unprecedented war situation, it is also coming as both a blessing as well as a challenge for both of us, for us as a manufacturer, because Indian factories are closed for some 300–400, so that will give you some respite in terms of products not coming in the countries.
At the same time, it is also putting a lot of pressure on us to suspend our supplies to countries where the sea we are using vessels to send material like Bahrain, Qatar, due to excessive charges levied by the shipping companies and also the ports amounting to $2000–3500 per container, which is excessively more than the cost of the product if you have to pay the duty, it becomes totally non-viable. That also applies to the incoming raw material which are coming, as you mentioned. Raw material we do have stocks, three months of stock to four months of stock, we do have. Also, there is no dearth of material coming in.
It can reflect in cost, and that, I believe it will be passed on to the market, because when the total industry as such will have the cost implication, it will definitely be reflecting in the net prices. That's what I see, that prices will be going up by next month, and that's where the recovery of cost implication of these factors of war surcharge and other things will be taken into account. That way, it's going to be the situation. We foresee that maybe it should not last more than two to three months. If it lasts more than three months, then the costs and also the prices will definitely see a very higher profit.
Abbas Al Lawati
SVP and Head of Project Management Office, Sohar International
Okay. Just to ask you on the capacity side now, you said you're targeting 80%-85% utilization for the year. What was the utilization last year?
Rajeev Singh
CEO, Al Maha Ceramics
72%.
Abbas Al Lawati
SVP and Head of Project Management Office, Sohar International
72%. Now, we were recently on the Al Anwar Ceramic call, and they have their ceramic capacity is 3x Al Maha's capacity. They are looking at a very strong year for Oman starting from Q1 itself. At least, that's the sense we got on the call. Now, Al Maha that has 1/3 capacity of Al Anwar Ceramic, I'm not sensing the same sort of enthusiasm from your side. I just want to understand, is it because Oman has not been an important market for you and maybe you've not made the same inroads like the Al Shams brand? I'm just trying to figure out what's going on with you guys versus, let's say, the positioning of Al Anwar Ceramic.
Rajeev Singh
CEO, Al Maha Ceramics
Okay, Abbas. Well, if you have seen me working, I've never taken Al Shams as our competition which I will follow. Because if you even see the profitability in the bottom line, we are much ahead than the Al Shams. Our objective is not to throw volume at unprecedented credit in the market. Rather, we are doing our business sensibly. You are right that throwing the material in the market just to gain the volume is easiest way approach. Then your prices and your profitability, you will see it will never come up. Rather, I'm trying to improve my product realization by introducing the products which can fetch good volume, good realization, and also the segments which value Italian, Spanish, and the products where the lifestyle and the mid and the upper mid segment of the customer we are targeting.
We are not into the masses where the commodity, because our capacity is low and we cannot have same strategy what my competition has. They have a pressure of volume. I don't have a pressure of volume. At the same time, I've just, for the heck of increasing my capacity utilization, I will not start throwing material at dirt cheap prices, where the cost and the selling prices are not making any sense. There are many markets which are asking for material, but the prices are ridiculously low and we can't go and just dispatch material to show utilization going up. I think end of the day, I have to see what bottom line we are going to get into.
If you see Oman market, as compared traditionally, our share of market in Oman was 40 versus 60 export, which has come up to 50%. Going forward, I look forward to have a much more strength in Oman market, wherein made in Oman products should be our key to visit all the government sites and the projects which are there clubbed with porcelain which we are producing. I think we should try to reach a bigger volume in Oman market, right? Challenges are also there coming in from export market like Yemen and also Saudi Arabia. Saudi Arabia 12.5% duty which is still there and refund not coming to any of the suppliers is one of the biggest challenge.
Ridiculously low prices by local Chinese there, is not making any sense to go to such a huge market. If you see my results, if I compare myself in 2020, I was selling almost close to 100,000 in Saudi Arabia, which has come down to big zero. Where those material has gone? Definitely it has come to Oman, and it has come to the higher realization area like UAE. I am selecting my market where to sell rather than just throwing endless, you know, blindly all the market. Secondly, Yemen is one change which has happened for the last seven to eight months, is that earlier money transfer was coming into cash and all. They have several routes to bring in the money when they were importing material from in any places.
Now, since last seven to eight months, the government has gone extremely strict in terms of what material we are importing, the rules and regulations, and also what money you are sending out of Yemen through Central Bank of Yemen, and then putting up a capping on the amount of money you can transfer in one time, lot of documentation, checking and all. These are one big hurdle which has brought our volume down in Yemen market also. Yemen was also 125,000–150,000 per month for us. Now we are trying to have an alternate market. As I told you, we are exploring new market. If you have seen our MD&A, we are the first Omani company to participate in Coverings 2026, which is the largest tile exhibition in United States of America.
US is one such market that even if we get a drop of it, I don't think we require to really dump our material in any of these territories. Frankly speaking, I am looking at the market which is suiting me rather than just going and, trying to be everywhere, right? I hope this answers your query.
Abbas Al Lawati
SVP and Head of Project Management Office, Sohar International
Yeah. Just my concern is on the export market, given what's going on, because you still rely 50% on export in Saudi. I hear you. I mean, that's the same feedback we've got from the other guys in the country, that Saudi pretty much exports are down to zero. Even without the customs duty, it's tough to compete with the Chinese there, with the local plants. Yemen, I've heard a similar story. That's the reason what the sense I got is Oman became more important in this context, especially with the anti-dumping duty in play and lower freight cost because obviously it's your home country. In your case, you're still looking at a 50% sort of thing outside Oman. Now, which market is that actually? Where you can make your realization?
Rajeev Singh
CEO, Al Maha Ceramics
Abbas, if you have seen the potential of the Gulf market, it is 500 million sq m, right? Oman does not play a very significant role in this potential. The largest market is Saudi Arabia, followed by UAE. Our next home base is UAE. If you have seen our market, we have been growing tremendously in UAE, and that is because of low logistic cost is also fetching better realization. This is a market which is for commodity to value-added to top-end products, everything is there. Frankly speaking, if you tap these two markets, you require at least three plants like Al Maha to exhaust, if you are really very strong in these markets, because the potential is so high.
You need not go and just put a glimpse of yourself in every of these territories and just spread out, keeping your credit risk and other things. Along with Oman, the next big market is UAE. Also as I told, we are exploring Jordan, some premium end customers we have already identified, and US is another market. To be honest, export market will definitely remain dynamic, keeping in view the tariff situation of US as well as present geopolitical situation. We have to be really like the opportunist in terms of which market is opening where, when. There cannot be a straight line which you can draw for the complete year because situation is unpredictable and it is dynamic.
Yes, you have got two strong markets, Oman and UAE, and the rest of the products you can decide when and where you want to sell.
Abbas Al Lawati
SVP and Head of Project Management Office, Sohar International
Okay, now if I speak about Al Hael, now you've written down the investment completely and obviously, we know your liability is limited to your investment. Now, when I see the notes, the company made a OMR 3.75 million comprehensive loss last year. But I believe Al Hael is still selling to you and then you're going and selling in the end market. This structure is still a bit lost on me. I'm a little confused. Can you elaborate the relationship, the partnership with Al Hael and what's going on? And obviously, what's the outlook for Al Hael in terms of both utilization and profitability when it comes to especially as Al Maha shareholders.
Rajeev Singh
CEO, Al Maha Ceramics
See, Al Hael has got a series of challenges. It's. When we took over, it came with a legacy of a series of court cases, liabilities, bank liabilities, and all. Definitely it was a tough task. There was a pause and leadership gap there for one year, which has put another pause for, say, one year. After I joined, I started the plant, and now it is running. Challenges are still there, because, to be honest, ease of doing business in Oman is not as it is elsewhere in other parts of the world. Getting visa, getting clearance, and getting one blockage after another, it's extremely difficult. What we planned versus what we are doing, we are trying to cross hurdles every day.
Now, since there was a very huge liability on Al Hael, bank was not ready to further extend, you know, benefits or, what, facilities to Al Hael, and also due to not very active participation from Qatari partners who still hold 55% of the share. The present arrangement is that Al Maha is marketing, selling, and strategizing the product strategy. We are buying everything from Al Hael. We are keeping a nominal profit on that, and then we are selling to the market, and that brings additional revenue as well as business opportunity for us.
In return, you can see that, when we will publish our results for this quarter, you can see that our sales are on an upward trend despite all challenges of manpower, raw material, and everything. There are huge orders which are piled up. Now porcelain is the future, and I, as I explained in my presentation, we are looking for starting Line 2 from the next three to four months' time with a value-added product fetching us margin about 25%-30%. That will give us much more leverage in terms of sustaining our business there. Yes, as far as the dividends and the profit to the company is concerned, it's not going to come.
Definitely, this product is going to help us penetrate new markets, sustain our footprints in the present market, and also help Al Maha to sell their products. Because single product, if you are taking to the customer, they have the choice to move to competition and then they can buy even ceramic from them. This is one thing which is like a symbiotic relationship, wherein Al Maha require Al Hael and we are selling Al Hael and it is giving us a premium segment. Our product of Al Hael fortunately surpasses the quality standards what even any of the local players have got, even the European. The products which have gone to the site, we have got repeated orders. We are commanding premium on the prices. Products are very good. This is well acceptable in the market.
I don't see any reason why I can't start Line 2 and if everything goes well, Line 3. Then we will sit back and decide how to reevaluate the whole things. Presently, so far so good. One line is going on. Second line is in process, maybe next three to four months depending on the situation of SL, because some of our CapEx things are stuck up in that.
Abbas Al Lawati
SVP and Head of Project Management Office, Sohar International
This Al Hael, when you speak about one line that's been operational, effectively you're working as a trader, right? They sell to you, they capture a small margin. You sell to the market, you capture a small margin. Now what is the quantity that we're looking at from this one line for, let's say, 2026?
Rajeev Singh
CEO, Al Maha Ceramics
How can you say that we are trader? We are managing the plant. Our team is managing the plant. We are producing. Don't get into the billing part. Billing can only you can see as a billing from A to B. I am very much in control of that plant. Even any screw in the plant, I am in control. Manpower, production, raw material, quality, design, productive strategy, everything is by Al Hael. It's not just like going and buying that stuff. We have plenty of choice in the market to go and do that. Why should we go to Al Hael then? As far as the capacity utilization is concerned, as I was telling you, the biggest issue what we are facing from ministry is the issuance of visa and the manpower. That is hindering our utilization of 100% utilization of Line 1.
Presently, around 125,000 per month is our production. We plan to take it to around 200,000 by next month. Once the Line 2 starts, gradually it should improve and take us to around 300,000–350,000 per month.
Abbas Al Lawati
SVP and Head of Project Management Office, Sohar International
Okay. Yes, I forgot that you are the one managing the plant. It's just that the nature of the relationship is that instead of Al Hael selling directly in the market, they're selling to Maha and Maha is selling in the market. That margin is being split between Maha and Al Hael, right? Because I'm a shareholder in Maha, not in Al Hael, obviously.
Rajeev Singh
CEO, Al Maha Ceramics
You should be happy.
Abbas Al Lawati
SVP and Head of Project Management Office, Sohar International
Yes. Are there any plans to recapitalize Al Hael?
Rajeev Singh
CEO, Al Maha Ceramics
Pardon me?
Abbas Al Lawati
SVP and Head of Project Management Office, Sohar International
Any plans to recapitalize Al Hael?
Rajeev Singh
CEO, Al Maha Ceramics
Not yet, but it is too early to comment on these matters, Abbas. I think the situation is dynamic. Let me sail through and run two lines successfully, then it will be a better time to discuss because all eyes are on us, including the eyes from the bank, and our shareholders, our board. We are having a very challenging task to move. But fortunately, I see lot of inquiries, market, and in orders pouring in, especially from UAE, the reputed top quality builders. Prices are not primary. The quality and the product taking the primary seat.
Since you are aware of porcelain is almost 70% of the market potential, and if only one plant is there, which is having the the top quality products which you can give to the market, I think you have a very high leverage to sell those products and get your margins.
Abbas Al Lawati
SVP and Head of Project Management Office, Sohar International
With the benefit of anti-dumping duty and now quality standards, will you become the preferred sort of porcelain tile by choice for the Omani ecosystem? Is that the endeavor?
Rajeev Singh
CEO, Al Maha Ceramics
See, the effect, as I told you, still has not started reflecting in. There are two things actually. Even the Quality Mark implementation is there from 1 March. The way SASO was implemented in Saudi Arabia in terms of absolutely zero tolerance, I think when it comes to Oman, it becomes little easy, and slowly we are pushing the ministry or the force that whether you are keeping an eye on these marks or not. I think presently, from 1 March it was implemented, and immediately the war is started. If this is the time when the gas supplies are suspended in most of the Indian plants.
Presently it's not really, we are able to say whether it is the closure of the plant or the implementation of this is affecting. As far as I know, it is because of suspension of the plants.
Abbas Al Lawati
SVP and Head of Project Management Office, Sohar International
That you're benefiting basically. Yes.
Rajeev Singh
CEO, Al Maha Ceramics
We should get benefit. Yeah.
Abbas Al Lawati
SVP and Head of Project Management Office, Sohar International
Now, if I just look at your cash flows, last year you were working at a 72% utilization and limited porcelain capacity from Al Hael and generated close to OMR 1.3 million in CFO. Obviously this year the guidance is based on the 80%-85% utilization you expect to hit by the end of the year. Things are looking obviously up. What sort of working capital are you looking at investment? Because I feel like Al Maha is practically debt-free, okay.
Rajeev Singh
CEO, Al Maha Ceramics
Yes.
Abbas Al Lawati
SVP and Head of Project Management Office, Sohar International
It could be a very interesting year from the company's perspective. There's operating leverage, obviously, right? Your costs are more or less, it's a low cost kind of fixed operating structure. When I model this, it looks like there could be a big sort of cash flow jump. I'm not sure what kind of working capital investment you're looking at. It could be an interesting sort of cash flow generating story for 2026. I just wanted to get your comments on that.
Vikas Shukla
Finance Manager, Al Maha Ceramics
Our cash flow, if you see, we are a really debt-free company.
Abbas Al Lawati
SVP and Head of Project Management Office, Sohar International
Yeah. It's actually debt-free. Yes.
Vikas Shukla
Finance Manager, Al Maha Ceramics
Yes. Why my cash scenario is changed because we increased our revenue as well as my raw material structure because earlier we are storing less working capital inventory. That we increase and we supporting to our Al Hael operation. That's why our cash flow, it means working capital is enhanced, occupied much more if you're comparing with the previous year. I'm hoping once our scenario become normal, so that will be definitely improved because if you see my doubtful debts and provision positions, it was much more improved in term of compare previous year.
Rajeev Singh
CEO, Al Maha Ceramics
I would like to comment here, Abbas, that the situation is so uncertain that presently, I cannot draw a line in terms of the deployment of working capital because, inventory, you don't know how long you have to keep and you have to store it if you are getting it at a consistent price. That is something unusual, right? Second, one thing we have to agree that overall the paying capacity and the rotation of money in the market has gone definitely very high, and if you can see it from competition, the name what you are referring, what, DSO they are operating. The best of the customers are also delaying the payment. It is a cycle which is overall affecting, like when you complete the cash generation.
If I really think of my first tenure of 2022 versus now, at least 30–60 days increase has been added in terms of rotation of money. That's something affecting the working capital. We are trying to manage. Our payments are also in terms of our vendors, if you see, that is well managed, and they have been also supporting in terms of increasing their credit periods. That's the situation so far. I think I can say that.
Abbas Al Lawati
SVP and Head of Project Management Office, Sohar International
Yeah, because I'm just thinking once your working capital kind of stabilizes, then all this cash flow can actually flow to shareholders. You know, given that you don't. Sorry.
Rajeev Singh
CEO, Al Maha Ceramics
Last six months since the war began. In fact, one after another, the situation is really not stabilizing.
Abbas Al Lawati
SVP and Head of Project Management Office, Sohar International
Right.
Rajeev Singh
CEO, Al Maha Ceramics
We really don't know how the situation will be and what measures one company has to take in terms of protect their interest and how the shift will happen in terms of one market to other based on, you know, the situation. Let's wait and watch. Presently, what I explained is the ground reality.
Abbas Al Lawati
SVP and Head of Project Management Office, Sohar International
Thank you, Rajeev. I think one comment from my side is, we look forward to these calls, and I think from what I know, and I track this company closely, is that you missed the half-yearly call in 2024. It's very important for investors to speak to people like you who obviously manage the company.
Rajeev Singh
CEO, Al Maha Ceramics
I have missed it, but I have not missed it with you, Abbas.
Abbas Al Lawati
SVP and Head of Project Management Office, Sohar International
No, I think the benefit of these calls is that MC has mandated companies to do these calls.
Rajeev Singh
CEO, Al Maha Ceramics
No, I appreciate. You know the challenges what I was going through. There were certain changes in terms of the head changes. That way I think I was single-handedly taking care of the operations.
Abbas Al Lawati
SVP and Head of Project Management Office, Sohar International
Yeah. I think.
Rajeev Singh
CEO, Al Maha Ceramics
That point is well under consideration.
Abbas Al Lawati
SVP and Head of Project Management Office, Sohar International
Yes. It's good to touch base again after the Q2 numbers, right? The half-yearly calls to see where we stand. Yes.
Rajeev Singh
CEO, Al Maha Ceramics
100%. 100% Abbas.
Abbas Al Lawati
SVP and Head of Project Management Office, Sohar International
Okay. Thank you, Rajeev. All the best.
Rajeev Singh
CEO, Al Maha Ceramics
Sorry. I think Sharief has been waiting from Visions.
Abbas Al Lawati
SVP and Head of Project Management Office, Sohar International
Yes. Thank you, Sharief
Sharief Abdulla
Research Analyst, Ubhar Capital
Yes. Hello, Mr. Rajeev. Thank you for the opportunity. I must admit it's a very interactive session, and that helps a lot. A lot of my questions have already been answered from what Abbas has been asking you. A couple of more things. To start with, I'll begin with the regional dynamics. Now, obviously we know that, imports and exports both into and from the region are now not as smooth as they were due to the ongoing conflict. My question is the region net importer or is it a net exporter? You mentioned that there's a 500 million sq m market for the whole GCC, and obviously with the export.
Imports not coming in, it gives you and other players the opportunity to sell in the region. But obviously with the regional players not being able to export, their inventory would also be there to sell. Just in terms of the overall numbers, is the region net importer or is it a net exporter? My question is, would the prices feel the pressure or not?
Rajeev Singh
CEO, Al Maha Ceramics
Can you repeat the last sentence? I couldn't hear it properly. What's your question?
Sharief Abdulla
Research Analyst, Ubhar Capital
My question is the GCC region a net importer of the ceramics and porcelain market? If so, then okay, you guys will be able to sell and there will still be demand for excess capacity. There won't be any excess capacity. If the region is a net exporter, as you mentioned, there's a 500 million sq m demand, but also there are some producers as well, right? Which export. If the region is a net exporter, then we might see some pressure on the prices because the exports are not really an option as it was before.
Rajeev Singh
CEO, Al Maha Ceramics
See, the situation is same for the years and years. If you talk about the previous years, earlier Chinese were dominating, then later on Indian companies took over the majority share. The commodity segment is always dominated by the mass suppliers coming from where the price really drives your market. In the first part of my answer to Abbas, I was actually explaining the same thing. If I position myself into the segment what you are talking, I definitely will be having a tremendous pressure all the time to look at my prices irrespective of what products we are trying to sell.
The competition, despite going for expansion and bigger size, value added, the generation of additional profit is missing only because the segmentation is poor and it is purely into commodity, where your value is getting dissipated just based on the prices. If I have to talk about Al Maha, I see very much a huge opportunity lying in upper mid, middle and niche segments where our brands are known for. That way it's a huge opportunity for us to carve our market share further in Oman as well as in UAE and whatever market we are talking.
Sharief Abdulla
Research Analyst, Ubhar Capital
Perfect. Great. Thank you. My next question is regarding your porcelain plant. We have seen close to OMR 800,000 sales from porcelain during 2025, and I believe that all belongs to Q4. What is the? You mentioned that now the Line 2 is opening, and you also mentioned that Al Hael started production in November. This OMR 800,000 revenue is for the last two months of 2025. Is that correct?
Rajeev Singh
CEO, Al Maha Ceramics
No, it is not correct. Plant, if you see, it was started in 2025 beginning.
Sharief Abdulla
Research Analyst, Ubhar Capital
Yeah.
Rajeev Singh
CEO, Al Maha Ceramics
It was in January. It then operated till end of March, middle of March. It was 2.5 months there and around two months here. It is around three to four months, what we are talking about. Frankly speaking, you are looking at revenue, which is giving you OMR 800,000, but you have to understand one thing that the prices are around 2x, if not 2x, at least 1.5x higher than the ceramic. If you translate this into square meter, the volume is around 5% of the total business. That means our operation has been just negligible. I will not say that there is a significant.
Yes, it is reflecting to OMR 800,000 because the average pricing around OMR 2.5–3 as compared to OMR 1.5 of ceramic. If you sell 100,000 of ceramic versus if you sell 50,000 of porcelain, the value is same. That way it is reflecting. Going forward, if I am consistent on my production and also operations, you can see much higher numbers of revenue coming in terms of our growth.
Sharief Abdulla
